excerpt: Greptile is an AI code review agent that automatically reviews every pull request with complete understanding of your codebase.
Every review comment includes a Fix with your Agent button that sends the issue — with file paths, line numbers, and suggested code — straight to Claude Code, Codex, Conductor, Cursor, or Devin.
A Fix All button in the review summary sends every issue at once.
Your 👍/👎 reactions and replies teach Greptile what matters. After 2-3 weeks, it stops commenting on things you don't care about.
Set up Greptile AI code reviews in 5 minutes. Connect GitHub or GitLab, configure review triggers, and get automated feedback on your first pull request.
Set up Greptile from your terminal with `greptile onboard` — or hand this page to your coding agent and have it run the setup for you.
Deploy Greptile in your own infrastructure with Docker Compose. Supports AWS, GCP, Azure, air-gapped environments, and custom LLM configurations.
Docker Compose: Up to 100 developers. Single VM, simpler operations. Kubernetes: 100+ developers. Horizontal scaling, high availability.
If your GitHub or GitLab instance restricts inbound traffic to specific IP addresses, you need to allowlist Greptile's IP range for code review to work.
Launch any agent in one click with a Greptile comment, full context, and suggested fix.
Access Greptile review comments, apply fixes, and manage coding patterns directly from your agent of choice.
View and resolve review comments directly from Claude Code.
Iteratively fix a PR until Greptile gives a perfect review: 5/5 confidence, zero unresolved comments.
Run `greptile review`, get a review of the feature branch diff in 60 seconds.

TREX runs your PR branch in a sandbox to find the bugs that only show up at runtime. It starts services, mocks inputs, clicks through UI flows, and leaves the logs, screenshots, and traces on the PR.
Control how strict Greptile is about leaving comments with the strictness setting (1–3).

Place `greptile.json` in your repository root. Settings are read from the source branch of the PR and override dashboard settings.
Fetch PR comments - Get unaddressed Greptile feedback for any PR
Connect Cursor, Claude Code, VS Code, or Codex to Greptile MCP with OAuth.
Greptile pairs static scanning with an AI security agent to catch vulnerabilities in every pull request.
v5 is faster, catches more bugs, and flags fewer false positives by running a swarm of narrowly scoped agents in parallel.
Greptile can now detect when a PR was authored by a coding agent and route the review to a different model. If Claude wrote it, GPT reviews it, and if GPT wrote it, Claude reviews it.

Security page, self-hosting and logging: "For self-hosted Greptile services, Custom Apps are hosted using your own infrastructure - such as on-premises - so that you and your users can build, run, and, use Greptile in your virtual private cloud (VPC)"; customers "can choose to also self-host LLMs" or bring their own; "Customers can choose to turn off logging and make chats 100% private. Note that in the self-hosted service, logs are stored on customer servers only."

Security page, De-Identified Data and AI Training (vendor's own carve-out): "Greptile may aggregate and anonymize Customer Data ('De-Identified Data') for analytical purposes and to monitor, improve, or expand our services, and may use such data to train and improve artificial intelligence algorithms and models ('AI Training and Learnings')."

Tested it on a Rails question they already knew the answer to (how BigDecimal is encoded by as_json). Greptile correctly said they're encoded as strings and pointed to active_support/core_ext/object/json.rb. The user said this 'would have saved me about 30mins of work.'
Tried generating sample code in the React repo and was 'pleasantly surprised' by the result.

Used it on their own C++ codebase. Impressed that it could identify which C++ standard was used, but found it 'really bad at analyzing templates.' Answers were 'always incomplete and usually at least partly or mostly incorrect,' even when comments in the source answered the question.
Disliked the 'Act on your behalf' GitHub permission Greptile requests. Another commenter suspected it wasn't needed and was 'just to harvest email addresses.'

Ran it on their OSS project (lofi). It was stuck at 99% loading for about 30 minutes, then every question returned 'Error: Internal error while locating sources.' A strange 'Onboard?' prompt also appeared. They called it 'pre-MVP quality' and said charging for it is 'highway robbery.'
'Not a single repo I've tried works.' Many repos never finished processing, and even the ones that did didn't work.

Several users hit failures: 'Error: Internal error while processing request.' on a personal public repo, 'This repo failed to process', and 'Internal error while locating sources' on a repo shown as green and up to date.
Querying public repos failed with an internal error after the user unlinked their GitHub connection. They argued it shouldn't need GitHub for public repos.
Possible bug with repos that have many branches. On datastax/cassandra, searching 'vsearch' showed CNDB-8708-vsearch and DSP-23946-vsearch but not the vsearch branch itself.
Couldn't use it because almost all their bioinformatics repos exceed 10MB due to test files. Didn't want to pay $20/month without a trial on their own large repo to judge quality.
Asking about the Porter repo returned 'Oops, We couldn't access this repo.' Another user linked GitHub but couldn't find where to enter the promo code.

'Looks good, but there are many competitors that do exactly the same thing (even opensource ones).' Others asked how it differs from Bloop, Cursor, and Adrenaline. One user wanted a local-only, self-hosted option.

'My employer uses greptile and I'm pretty happy with it. Sometimes it can be a bit overzealous but more often than not it catches real issues and gives the author a chance to reply or fix them before another human reviews the PR.'
Has no direct experience, but after asking a mailing list of engineering leaders about AI code review assistants, several suggested Greptile. The commenter called this hearsay that it works.

Responding to a post calling Greptile's new pricing predatory: competitors will likely make the same pricing changes. They found reports of OSS contributors being billed 'unfortunate,' since Greptile had earned goodwill with its free OSS offer and it would be a shame if it weren't following through.
